display.title: The Tzemach Tzedek and the Dancing That Saved a Child (Adar)
display.summary_short: For the month of Adar: why simcha should keep doubling, the young Rebbe Maharash's clever giggle, and a Chassid whose dancing on Simchas Torah broke a harsh decree.
display.summary_long: After a short greeting, the storyteller opens with the song "I believe in Hashem" and celebrates the month of Adar. Quoting the Zohar, he explains that when a Jew smiles, Hashem smiles back, and that marbin b'simcha means doubling one's joy every day, illustrated with a riddle: a penny doubled for thirty days beats a thousand dollars. A short story follows: the young Rebbe Maharash giggles whenever his teacher enters, and tells his father, the Tzemach Tzedek, that he is following the Gemara's words about Adar and Av with a Yiddish twist. The main story: a Chassid's son is gravely ill, and the father reaches Lubavitch on Hoshana Rabbah. The Tzemach Tzedek gives only a vague brachah, and the father weeps over Tehillim. When the hakafos begin on Shemini Atzeres, he realizes Hashem wants him to rejoice, and he forces himself to dance with all his strength through Simchas Torah. Before he leaves, the Tzemach Tzedek tells him there had been a decree that no brachah could change, but his simcha broke it. He comes home to a healthy son. The listeners are urged to bring music and dancing into their homes all Adar.
display.lesson: Simcha breaks through decrees and brings brachos; even when you are worried, act joyful and real joy will follow. In Adar we keep increasing our simcha.

advisories.note: A child is gravely ill and the doctors give up hope; he recovers completely.

characters: a Chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek

sources_cited.note: When a Jew is joyful, Hashem shines joy back to him (as cited).
Mishenichnas Adar marbin b'simcha; mishenichnas Av mematin b'simcha.
A maamar of the Rebbe from 5746: in our generation we serve Hashem with simcha rather than tears.
